title: Police seize limited edition £3.7m Ferrari in supercar crackdown
description: Rare £3.7m Ferrari seized in police crackdownImage source, Met PoliceImage caption, This Ferrari Monza is one of only 499 vehicles of this typeA Ferra
body: Rare £3.7m Ferrari seized in police crackdownImage source, Met PoliceImage caption, This Ferrari Monza is one of only 499 vehicles of this typeA Ferrari valued at about £3.7m was among 90 vehicles seized by police during a weekend operation against antisocial driving in central London.The Metropolitan Police said the vehicles, worth more than £8m in total, were taken in Kensington, Chelsea and Hyde Park between Friday and Sunday. Officers targeted uninsured, antisocial and dangerous driving.The Ferrari Monza SP2 is one of 499 built by the Italian manufacturer and had been in the UK for a day when it was stopped, the force said.The Met said the driver had been in the car for less than half an hour, held only a provisional licence and had no insurance.Image source, Met PoliceImage caption, A Black Rolls-Royce, yellow Lamborghini, green Mercedes and black BMW parked side by side after being seizedA Monza SP2 sold at auction for £3.7m ($4.9m) earlier this year.Fifteen vehicles were taken under powers that allow officers to seize a car immediately where it has been used antisocially, rather than issue a warning first.Special Ch Insp Geoff Tatman, who led the operation, said: "We regularly hear from local people who are fed up with people driving cars dangerously in the area, or with modifications which make them a nuisance to those who live nearby."He said seizing vehicles was intended to keep roads safe and deter dangerous driving.Image source, Met PoliceImage caption, A Lamborghini Revuelto is taken away on a police recovery truck at Wellington ArchOfficers also arrested a man on suspicion of handling stolen goods and money laundering after finding 19 bank cards in other people's names and more than £2,500 in cash, the Met said.A second man, stopped on suspicion of driving without insurance, was arrested on suspicion of possessing drugs with intent to supply.Two further arrests were made, one on suspicion of using words or behaviour likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress, and one on suspicion of an immigration offence.The Met said the number and value of the vehicles seized was the highest in the five years the operation has run.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Dakota Ditcheva says she has broken both hands again
description: Dakota Ditcheva says she has "cried non-stop" after breaking both of her hands in the win over Denise Kielholtz - just months after recovering from si
body: Dakota Ditcheva says she has "cried non-stop" after breaking both of her hands in the win over Denise Kielholtz - just months after recovering from similar injuries.The Briton outclassed Kielholtz at PFL New York earlier this month to win by unanimous decision in her first fight in just over a year.The 28-year-old had not fought since July 2025 as a result of breaking her left hand - then suffered a fracture in her other hand five months later.Despite comfortably beating Kielholtz on her return, Ditcheva says she fought the majority of the contest with two broken hands."I broke my hands in the fight. I could feel it from the second I started the second round," she said on YouTube., external "I didn't tell my corner. I didn't tell anybody. I didn't show it this time, and I didn't actually tell anybody until I got out of the cage."I am back in splints until my surgeon has decided what the next steps are going forward, which will be in the next few days."Ditcheva, who extended the unbeaten start to her career to 16 fights, said one of her injuries occurred after opting not to have surgery on it last year while the other is a "small break on the other finger that didn't hold up so well"."The good thing is I have no new breaks. It's just the hand that wasn't operated on that I broke at the end of last year," added Ditcheva."I was told that if I didn't go ahead with surgery at that time, there was a possibility it could break again. I took the risk in not doing the surgery because I was hoping it would hold strong, and it didn't."So therefore I'm paying the price for it now and I will be out for a little bit."

schema.headline: Dakota Ditcheva says she has broken both hands again

title: Thames Water gave finance chief a £1m signing-on fee
description: Thames Water paid its finance chief a £1m signing-on fee in July as the company struggles with a mountain of debt and faces temporary nationalisation.
body: Thames Water paid its finance chief a £1m signing-on fee in July as the company struggles with a mountain of debt and faces temporary nationalisation.Steve Buck joined the company in April 2025 but it is understood the seven-figure payment was not made until last month after the company had taken legal advice over its contractual obligations.The existence of the payment, first reported by Sky News,, external was revealed in a letter from the Thames Water chairman to MPs on the Commons Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee.In the letter,, external Sir Adrian Montague said he understood customers would see large payments to senior leaders as "unjust" but argued they were necessary to stop staff leaving.The letter said: "The majority of the team were brought in recently to fix the problems the company faces and are not responsible for causing those problems."These talented and experienced individuals have opportunities for roles outside Thames Water and, in many cases, have been actively approached by other companies. "These roles would be less in the public gaze, less difficult and more remunerative."Sir Adrian described the payment to Buck as a "necessary incentive" and said the money had come from emergency funding provided by Thames Water's lenders.He said the company is facing recruitment and retention difficulties and warned the problem would "persist" if it was nationalised or put into special administration. Alistair Carmichael, Lib Dem MP and chair of the Environment Committee, said: "Money should be going into improving services, not remunerating already well-paid senior executives."The government were clear in the early days that they wanted this to stop. It is obvious that they have not succeeded in this.  We need to hear now from them about what they intend to do about it."The utility company owes roughly £20bn and has been working with creditors and government officials to find a way forward.Failure to reach a deal could lead to Thames Water being forced into a "special administration regime", a form of temporary nationalisation intended to keep the business operating until a viable solution can be found.This would see government-appointed officials temporarily running the company – including funding its operations and upgrading infrastructure as well as dealing with any outstanding debts following a restructuring of the business.If the company was subsequently sold to a private buyer, the government would be able to recoup some taxpayer cash.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he would like to see "greater public control" of key water and energy utilities.In the past year, Thames Water boss Chris Weston saw his pay increase 14% to £1.63m while other directors received bonuses totalling £4.1m. Speaking on the BBC Big Boss interview late last month, Weston acknowledged there was anger about Thames Water pay, but argued that the company needed to be able attract "capable people to help turn this company around". "If we're not prepared to pay market rates, then they won't come to us and they won't stay with us," he said.Weston also warned special administration could see taxpayers left bearing the cost. Instead, he threw his weight behind a rescue deal that has been put forward by the firm's lenders. Thames Water has faced intense criticism for several years over failures to prevent sewage discharges and leaks.Last year it was handed a record fine of £122.7m from the regulator Ofwat, who said the company had "let down its customers and failed to protect the environment". Weston said he wanted the company to "do better" but some of the targets it had been set were "not realistic". Thames Water has warned it only has enough cash to last until the end of the year, putting pressure on the new government to decide what to do with the company, which provides water to 16 million people across London and the Thames Valley.Ministers could give the green light to the rescue deal, proposed by Thames Water's lenders, which would see some debts written off and new money invested in exchange for leniency on environmental targets.The previous Environment Secretary Emma Reynolds dismissed the plan as weak, arguing it did not do enough for consumers. She has since been replaced by Angela Eagle.

schema.headline: Thames Water gave finance chief a £1m signing-on fee

title: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week
description: For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools h
body: For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools have insisted that the technology will ultimately mean people will spend less of their time working.An engineering director at Google said four years ago that AI would deliver a four-day work week by 2025, external.Earlier this year, and just one year after that engineering director's prediction, OpenAI took up the challenge, in a manner of speaking. It formally urged companies to start testing out a four-day work week (with no change in pay), claiming that AI will soon be able to speed up so much human labour that the corporate world should prepare itself.However, a former OpenAI technical employee who left the company last year told the BBC the firm never actually trialled the four-day work week it suggested others should try while they were there.Instead, the person described what was often a gruelling work culture marked by frequent "crisis meetings", working on weekends, and "super cut-throat" performance reviews that would see colleagues suddenly let go."You go in on Saturday or Sunday just to catch up or make sure things aren't broken," the person said.Other companies have also pushed the idea that AI will effectively reduce the number of hours people need to work, for better or worse.Anthropic has boasted that its popular coding tool and chatbot Claude is capable of working on its own for seven hours without a break, external, essentially a full corporate workday. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg has said his company is in the middle of the year when "AI starts to dramatically change the way that we work" and that such tools let far fewer employees do more than they ever could have before.While Meta has since laid off 1 in 10 of its employees, Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that as AI tools inevitably become more productive, it could mean, external even broader job losses.Despite these claims, workers inside these same tech companies, who are not only developing but using the very AI tools that will purportedly perform at least some of people's work, say they are clocking in far more than the typical five-day, 40-hour work week.US tech workers are typically well-compensated, external, and while other industries such as investment banking, law and medicine also often see people work long hours, a 14-hour workday was not always the norm in tech. For years, it was a more typical 9-5 office job.But the former OpenAI employee said they would put in at least 70 hours a week, much more than they did in previous tech jobs. The person now works at a start-up also focused on AI, and said their work-life balance has improved, working closer to 50-60 hours a week, "outside of sprints".A "sprint" is term for a common period in technology companies in which people work long hours in the weeks leading up to a release of a new feature or product.Inside AI companies and larger tech companies working furiously on AI projects, however, such sprints can be extreme. At OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, sprints can stretch on for many weeks and top 90 hours of work in a seven-day period, tech workers that the BBC spoke to for this story said.Neither company responded to BBC requests for comment. At Meta, workers said they have been abruptly pushed onto teams this year doing AI work being treated as urgent. They called it being "drafted", according to one current and one former employee, because people were not given a choice."They just move you over," the former employee said. "You can't say no – or if you do, you have to quit."They said although Meta recently began to walk back, external that strict take it or leave us approach, by then many workers had already been forced onto such work.The hours on such teams at Meta are often long, with staff working into the night, on weekends, and feeling they are "on call" during the hours they are not working, according to descriptions of the work from the current and former employees.There are no limits, external in the US on how many hours a person over the age of 16 can work. In the UK and Europe, for instance, laws limit a working week to 48 hours, including overtime.Meta's current AI projects include the creation of an AI tool that can be used for software engineering and other kinds of work, and building AI model infrastructure that can measure an AI model's success in replicating various tasks, the employees added."You're literally working in teams of people trying to replicate humans doing jobs," the former employee said.That work, the person added, seems "endless".A Meta spokesperson declined to comment.Even tech workers who are not directly involved in the development of AI tools are facing longer hours due to the technology.A former Google employee, Amin Shali, left the company in May due to the ways in which he claimed AI was negatively impacting his job, like having to often work all hours of the night because internal engineering functions had failed. This was happening more frequently as Google moved crucial resources like processing units and memory storage over to AI projects.A Google spokesperson declined to comment.Since leaving Google, Shali told the BBC that his sleep and overall health had improved. He said he's realised that heavy reliance on AI tools in large tech companies "creates a bad culture with excess pressure on engineers".Some new research suggests that AI tools are making people's workloads even more burdensome.A study, external out of UC Berkeley followed hundreds of workers at a US tech company for eight months as they used AI. It found the employees "worked at a faster pace, took on a broader scope of tasks, and extended work into more hours of the day".Neil Thompson, an innovation scholar at MIT, said that even at tech companies leading on AI development, it is unlikely that workers are being told to simply deploy the tools that are supposed to do some of their work and move on."It leads to a situation where even if there were real time savings, it would be sucked up by the changes, and implementing them, and making sure they worked," Thompson said.The UC Berkeley research found that the workload of tech employees was expanded in part because of the need to constantly check the output of AI tools.In a situation where an employee had smoothed out processes for AI tools, people also tend to fill any time saved with more work, Thompson added, either because they want to or they feel they should do in order to prove their value to an employer."People assume that 20% less work means four-day weeks," Thompson said. "But new work emerges."As Shali observed: "AI is supposed to be doing so much for us now, so many more people should at least have better health and better sleep."Instead, it seems to be the opposite.

schema.headline: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa accused of breaking trust 'through deception'
description: Infantino broke trust 'through deception' - confederation presidentsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, FIFA president Gianni Infantino was first
body: Infantino broke trust 'through deception' - confederation presidentsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, FIFA president Gianni Infantino was first elected in 2016ByFootball issues correspondentFifa and its president Gianni Infantino have been accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation.The letter, signed by the presidents and general secretaries of the three regional governing bodies, said recent controversy over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was fundamentally about "the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it".FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including the World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.It was aborted after widespread criticism from several confederations, led by Uefa which has threatened a boycott of all Fifa competitions.BBC Sport understands that there have been preliminary discussions between the three confederations over breakaway competitions - should Infantino remain in situ."When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned," the letter read.It added: "Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding - or demanding - power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it."While the statement did not name Infantino, sources have told BBC Sport that it should be seen as an opportunity for him to resign and leave his position with dignity.It comes after Fifa issued a statement on Saturday evening which strongly criticised a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and Infantino.'Proposal inherently wrong... a profound failure of judgement'The three confederations - representing Europe, North America, Central America and the Caribbean, and Asia - criticised a statement released by Fifa after Infantino called management board members to a meeting in Rabat, Morocco last Wednesday.The confederations cited Infantino shutting out FIFA council members and member associations from the meeting, instead summoning only Fifa-employed senior staff.The open letter added that Fifa's admission of mistakes made in the FFE process did not go far enough."It did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong," the letter stated. "There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the Fifa World Cup was a profound failure of judgement."Not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions Fifa exists to serve."Fifa has committed to presenting a report to the next meeting of the Fifa council, which is expected to take place in October.But the three confederations said this failed to "recognise that proper governance in the face of such a profound lack of judgement would require that such a review be conducted by a fully independent third party".Their letter added: "There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness."It also underlined a legal warning made by Uefa that Fifa should not delete or destroy any documents related to the abandoned plans.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Barely three weeks have passed since the World Cup final was stagedCould breakaway competitions be created?Uefa last week insisted that Fifa's defence of Infantino "changes nothing" about a potential boycott of competitions.The three confederations have considered possible breakaway competitions, but they have provided no detail on what they could look like or when they would begin.The parties behind the open letter made the case that "football's strength has always been its unity" and said that it had been written "not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve".They added: "We call for that unity to be honoured now, for leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it."But so far Concacaf and Asia have not publicly committed to a possible boycott. And within those confederations opposition to Infantino is not assured.Among Concacaf nations, Mexico last week came out in support of the Fifa president.Of the 46 AFC members, so far eight countries have publicly backed Infantino - United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Sri Lanka, Lebanon, Kuwait, Mongolia, the Philippines and Bhutan.The first test of Uefa's threat is just over three weeks away, when the Fifa Under-20 Women's World Cup is due to kick off. It is being hosted by Poland and features five other European nations, including England.Last week, France said they are still planning to compete.Analysis: Ramping up pressure in football's civil warBySports editorThis is a potentially significant development.According to sources close to the rebellion against Infantino, they are now sending him a clear message: resign now and leave your position with dignity, rather than seek re-election in March.Alongside this joint statement, I am told the three confederations have begun preliminary discussions about organising competitions among themselves, so that players can still compete even if there is a boycott of Fifa tournaments such as next month's U20 Women's World Cup.Since this crisis began, Asia has been seen as a key battleground, a region that could determine whether Infantino stays in power.Some of the 46 countries in this vast region have said they still support Infantino. But the fact that the AFC president Sheikh Salman has signed off this letter suggests he is confident that there are plenty of others who want change.Infantino still retains the support of South America, Africa, and indeed Mexico within Concacaf. But is that enough?If UEFA and Concacaf voted as a bloc (with a few exceptions) against him, it would only need around a third of the AFC to join them to win any vote.But could a candidate capable of challenging Infantino and unifying the game be found?The fact those behind the revolt are so keen for him to step down suggests they are still not sure they would have enough votes.What is clear is that this latest solidifying of the rebellion against Infantino ramps up the pressure on him once again in world football's unprecedented civil war.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa accused of breaking trust 'through deception'

title: Kamal on making music for 'real ones' and Dave collaboration
description: "Dave is such a humble guy and he doesn't feel too inaccessible because I feel like he really leads from a love of music, first and foremost," says Ka
body: "Dave is such a humble guy and he doesn't feel too inaccessible because I feel like he really leads from a love of music, first and foremost," says Kamal. "Which is the exact same way that I feel."Dave featuring on his album is a full circle moment as Kamal previously featured on the rapper's 2021 track Mercury. "I feel like the connection was already established for the most part," Kamal says of their relationship."But yeah, it still feels scary when you hit him up because you're like, obviously it is Dave, I grew up listening to him so it feels like a massive moment."Rapper Dave, who has numerous Brit Awards, Ivor Novellos and a Mercury Prize to his name, opens up Kamal's track, The People That Saved Me, with poignant lyrics about love and memories.Kamal says the verse was "perfect for the album" and "the kind of message" he wanted to send. He has also featured on Mobo award-winning rapper Central Cee's 2025 track Now We're Strangers, and joined him on stage at London's The O2 to perform it. "I feel like the O2 is a dream venue for so many of us musicians so to be up there was proper surreal," he says of that moment.Amidst the major collaborations, Kamal wants to create music that is meaningful - something which comes across in his work. "The music is always going to be the leading factor and you don't even get the co-signs unless there's a little something there in the first place," Kamal says. And he plans to keep his day one fans at the forefront of it all. "For the people that really love my music, they see the common thread, separately of those external things, of really vulnerable writing, which is what I always try and lead with," he explains. "I always say I try and lead with honesty in the music, and I feel like that's the best way I can express myself."The people that latch onto that are always the real ones at the core of the fan base."The singer's 13-track album also includes songs like Suffer, which explores topics around love and heartbreak, and All My Favourite People Are Sad, which talks of depression and friendship. It's a lot of reflection for someone so young, and includes experimental tones which add a different layer to his usual soft singing voice. Kamal describes his background as a mix of Trinidad, Belize, English and Palestinian and his childhood was filled with music.But his relationship with music came before any hopes he might have had about making it big - and he says he still has much to learn. "I feel like there's still a long way to go when I look at my music career, but I'm also very grateful for everything that's happened so far," he says.

schema.headline: Kamal on making music for 'real ones' and Dave collaboration

title: Ban on 'subscription traps' brought forward by three months
description: Subscriptions will be easier to cancel and companies will be compelled to make it clear when contracts auto-renew at a higher price, Andy Burnham has
body: Subscriptions will be easier to cancel and companies will be compelled to make it clear when contracts auto-renew at a higher price, Andy Burnham has announced.The prime minister is also planning to outlaw shops from falsely claiming products previously retailed at much higher prices to advertise supposed deals, which he said tricks shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.Burnham will bring forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to end so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices".Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.On subscriptions, the government said the changes will mean businesses have "to provide clearer up-front information, regular reminders and a much easier exit to contracts" for customers. Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers £400m a year in total, or up to £170 per person.At the time, the Department for Business and Trade said there are 10 million unwanted, active subscriptions across the UK.It said that more than 3.5 million people are being "quietly rolled from free or discounted trials into fully costed contracts", while another 1.3 million are caught out by unexpected auto-renewals.On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.Consumer group Which? said it has "repeatedly exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren't what they seem".Its head of consumer rights policy, Sue Davies, welcomed the announcement and called for the government to bring the rules in "swiftly".But Stride said: "The cost of living didn't become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government." The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act, passed under the Conservatives in 2024, cracked down on hidden fees, fake reviews online and made it easier for customers to cancel subscriptions. It is already unlawful to use false "was" prices for items on sale, but it is not on the list of the Competition and Markets Authority's (CMA) list of banned practices.Practices on the list, such as operating pyramid schemes or displaying a quality assurance mark without authorisation, are automatically considered illegal without consumer harm having to be proved.The Liberal Democrats urged Burnham to "go further" to protect consumers, with Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper calling for "strengthened protections against rogue traders" and action to tackle supermarket "shrinkflation" — the practice of products being made smaller yet being sold for the same price. The announcement is Burnham's latest intervention aimed at easing the cost of living, following a £2 bus fare cap in England and a VAT cut on household electricity bills.But he is likely to come under pressure to make more significant changes in the Budget, which will be delivered by Chancellor John Healey on 28 October.But Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.

schema.headline: Ban on 'subscription traps' brought forward by three months

title: Record 230 people cross English Channel in one small boat
description: There have been signs that smugglers are putting more and more people into each boat. In 2018, there was an average of seven people per boat - but las
body: There have been signs that smugglers are putting more and more people into each boat. In 2018, there was an average of seven people per boat - but last year, that had risen to 62.On Tuesday, 173 migrants had to be rescued from a single boat, which caught fire. However, the number of crossings overall is on course to be lower this year.So far, the number of migrants who have made the crossing is down by 43%. The number of boats that have successfully crossed is down by 49%.Last month, the Home Office recorded the lowest number of crossings in July since 2020.Officials think this is partly because they have managed to disrupt the supply of small boats and engines to the people smugglers, with 1,100 seized since Labour came to power.Officials claim that with the sophisticated surveillance and reconnaissance operation now operating over the Channel, "unintercepted" beach landings have ended.All boats that make it across the halfway point in the Channel are met at sea by Border Force, which then brings the migrants safely ashore for processing.There is still clear demand for the crossings as the number of people waiting in camps in northern France has not reduced. At the same time, weather conditions have not been significantly different this year.Officials believe this shows their work to disrupt the smuggling gangs is beginning to show results. Despite this, concerns persist about the numbers still able to make it across the Channel. The English Channel is one of the most dangerous, and busiest, shipping lanes in the world.Many migrants come from some of the poorest and most chaotic parts of the world, and ask to claim asylum once they are picked up by the UK authorities.On a recent visit to Dover, the prime minister pledged his government would be "relentless" in curbing the number of small boat arrivals.Andy Burnham said enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs had been doubled on both sides of the Channel, but "a system that offers safe routes for people" needed to be built as well.In April, the UK and France struck a £662m (773m euro) deal aiming to address the issue.The three-year agreement included plans to send riot-trained police to French beaches to tackle violence and "hostile crowds", as well as France deploying millions of pounds worth of drones and two helicopters as part of a system to intercept people smugglers and illegal migrants.On X, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "At 2.30am this morning a boat carrying 230 people was taken into Dover."This is a record number in a single vessel."It's yet more proof that this illegal invasion is a national security emergency."Earlier on Monday, a Home Office spokesperson said: "We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020."But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJessica RawnsleyThe world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJessica RawnsleyThe world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific, according to the EU's climate monitoring service.The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023.Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region.Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week, as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought.Around Europe, sea surface temperatures in July reached record highs along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread strong and severe marine heatwaves.Sea temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific, where El Niño conditions are developing and forecast to strengthen in the coming months. El Niño is a natural weather pattern in the Pacific that combined with human-driven global warming can cause temperature spikes and more extreme weather.Oceans are a vital regulator of the climate, absorbing most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gas emissions and producing half of Earth's oxygen.The greatest effect of ocean warming is on sea level rise. As seawater warms it expands, and this thermal expansion accounts for roughly a third of sea level rise recorded by scientists to date. That water encroaches on low-lying coasts and island nations.Hotter seas are also driving longer and fiercer marine heatwaves, which have bleached coral reefs on a mass scale and decimated kelp forests and fisheries.Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, intensifying tropical storms and loading them with heavier rainfall.'Climate change is intensifying heat extremes'Western Europe is experiencing an exceptional run of extreme heat - with record-breaking temperatures in June and July, and some areas facing their third or fourth heat wave since May.The average temperature across western Europe for June and July was 21.62C - 2.79C above average and the highest for the two-month period."July 2026 was the third consecutive month of exceptional heat in western Europe," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over the region, she said, while dry soils reduced the ability to provide natural cooling."This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," she added.France, Spain, parts of Germany and the UK recorded exceptionally low rainfall and/or soil moisture, while soil moisture levels across much of western Europe were significantly lower than in 2022, when the region experienced severe drought.River levels have been much lower than average - in some places exceptionally low -with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among those particularly affected.Low flows exacerbate pressure on water supplies and irrigation, aquatic ecosystems, river transport and energy production.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Some rivers in Europe have recorded extremely low water levels, including the Danube The prolonged hot and dry conditions have created favourable conditions for wildfires, with massive wildfires raging across western Europe last month and "exceptional activity" in terms of the area burned and smoke and emissions generated."Climate change is increasingly bringing the kinds of hot and dry conditions that favour large, high-intensity wildfires in southern Europe while extended the fire season northwards," said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.Larger fires produce more smoke and inject it higher into the atmosphere, allowing it to travel much further, he said.That means countries that experience relatively few wildfires could be increasingly affected by smoke traveling long distances.Extreme weather 'new normal'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, European wildfires haven been called "completely unprecedented" this summerIn the UK, meanwhile, the prolonged dry spell is increasing pressure on already-stretched water supplies.England and Wales recorded their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, while large parts of England and all of Wales have already been officially declared in drought.The Environment Agency has warned that more areas of England could be declared in drought if dry conditions persist.Weather that was once considered extreme is becoming the "new normal", according to the latest Met Office report on the UK's climate.Its latest assessment found that the hottest day of the year in southern England is now 4.5C warmer than it was between 1961 and 1990."We are right now living in a time of historic and unprecedented change," said Mike Kendon, Met Office climate information scientist, adding that "evidence shows the climate of the 20th century has now gone".Scientists say El Niño may temporarily push global temperatures even higher. Its effects are being felt against a backdrop of man-made warming, particularly the burning of fossil fuels.The world is now about 1.4C warmer on average than it was in the late 19th Century.

schema.headline: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures

title: Championship all-stars to global gamble – will Ipswich Town's approach work?
description: Newly promoted Ipswich Town have quietly been the Premier League's fourth-biggest net spenders so far this summer, behind only Chelsea, Tottenham and
body: Newly promoted Ipswich Town have quietly been the Premier League's fourth-biggest net spenders so far this summer, behind only Chelsea, Tottenham and Arsenal.Ten players have joined for a combined £106.6m, but what is most notable about the Tractor Boys' approach under new manager Gary O'Neil is the sea change in recruitment strategy, shaped by lessons learned from their chastening single season in the top flight in 2024-25.Under O'Neil's popular predecessor Kieran McKenna, who stepped down on 10 June after overseeing three promotions in four full seasons, the Blues targeted players familiar with English football.McKenna's success was built mainly on players from the UK and Republic of Ireland, supplemented by a handful of overseas additions already accustomed to the language and culture through spells at other English clubs.Ipswich made 39 permanent first-team signings during McKenna's four-and-a-half-year reign, 32 of them either born or raised in Britain or Ireland, with just two joining directly from European clubs.But the premium on domestic talent makes it difficult, if not impossible, to bridge the gulf between the Championship and Premier League. The success of Sunderland and Leeds last season demonstrated that for promoted teams to thrive, finding value in the transfer market is essential. When Ipswich last went up in 2024, 10 of their 12 summer signings were British or Irish players acquired from other English sides.This time, the Blues have cast their net far wider, with Emersonn and Florentino Luis set to be the first Brazilians to represent the club, Sasa Lukic the first Serbian and Daizen Maeda the first Japanese player.Of the 10 players purchased, the only Briton is Chuba Akpom from Ajax. Even his arrival is an anomaly, given Ipswich were obliged to buy him following promotion despite an underwhelming loan spell.Ipswich's previous recruitment model can be traced back to their four seasons in League One.After guiding Town back to the Championship in 2023, McKenna admitted the club had made a "conscious decision" not to target overseas players because of the fast and frantic nature of England's third tier.A largely unchanged – but tightly knit – squad then exceeded expectations by finishing second in the Championship in 2023-24, making Ipswich the first side in 12 years to reach the Premier League through back-to-back promotions.At that point, the Blues' hierarchy could have ripped up the modus operandi that had served them so well and pivoted towards more extensive overseas recruitment. Instead, they doubled down on the approach, focusing mainly on emerging domestic talent largely unproven beyond the Championship. A £100m summer spending spree brought Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O'Shea and Jacob Greaves to Portman Road – players who had primarily shone in the second tier but were identified as having the potential to develop into established Premier League performers.Mindful that the odds were against survival, Ipswich also targeted players thought unlikely to baulk at remaining part of the project in the event of relegation.This time around, chairman Mark Ashton says Ipswich have to be "a bit braver" in their approach to the Premier League, and the type of players the club are pursuing reflects that increased ambition.Japanese attacker Maeda and Morocco centre-back Issa Diop were both on target at the World Cup this summer, and a third goalscorer from that tournament could follow.The Tractor Boys have been linked with a move for Paraguayan forward Julio Enciso, who played under O'Neil at Strasbourg last season and had an injury-blighted loan spell at Portman Road during the second half of 2024-25.While McKenna had enough credit in the bank to play the long game, O'Neil knows he needs to forge a competitive side quickly."Two seasons ago, the club didn't get anywhere near staying in the division and this time we need to do better," he said last month. "That's why we're trying to add quality to the squad from different parts of the world and we're trying to add some different attributes."The former Bournemouth and Wolves boss indicated after Saturday's 3-0 win against Rayo Vallecano that more incomings are likely, saying the "plan is to do quite a bit more".Ashton acknowledges that one of the key lessons from their previous Premier League campaign was the need to bring in more athletic players "with a different set of physical attributes".The midfield lacked power and ball-winning ability in 2024-25, and it is imperative that new arrivals Florentino Luis and Sasa Lukic – both experienced at the highest level – hit the ground running. That will be especially important with last season's mainstays Azor Matusiwa and Jack Taylor doubtful for the opening game following operations over the summer.It is no surprise that O'Neil is also seeking greater cutting edge given that no Ipswich player scored more than 10 non-penalty goals in the Championship last season.The Blues broke their transfer record to sign Brazilian striker Emersonn, 22, for an initial £24m. He certainly fits the desired physical profile but is relatively raw, having only established himself as a regular last season at Toulouse, where he scored seven goals in 31 appearances, 22 of them starts.Maeda, a hardworking forward or winger, had an excellent record at Celtic, netting 79 times in 212 games, but won't get the same volume of chances in a team battling to stay up.The Suffolk side have also recruited two Dutch goalkeepers, including Kjell Scherpen, whose imposing 6ft 9in (2.06m) frame means he is set to become the tallest player to appear in the Premier League.With a new manager in place and a £30m training ground redevelopment close to completion, this could be a defining summer for Ipswich. But will their transfer business be enough to secure successive top-flight campaigns for the first time in a quarter of a century?Only three promoted clubs have splashed out more in a summer window – Sunderland in 2025, Nottingham Forest in 2022 and Aston Villa in 2019 – and all survived. Yet Fulham, Southampton, Burnley and Ipswich themselves have spent comparable figures in recent years only to swiftly return to the Championship - with that level of investment increasingly the bare minimum needed to be competitive rather than a guarantee of safety.

schema.headline: Championship all-stars to global gamble – will Ipswich Town's approach work?

title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
description: A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says
body: A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear – plus a tie for secondary schools.Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.The government says the changes will save some families "up to £50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was £101.94 with a pinafore, and £83.95 without – but this year it will cost families an average of £53.97. Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms. Because every school sets its own uniform policy, parents can still face very different expectations and costs.Lorraine, who lives in London, has two children in secondary schools and is frustrated that her school has not changed any of its uniform policy this year.She says several items are still compulsory, including the branded blazer, tie, branded polo shirt, branded shorts and two-toned PE socks.Even the plain grey trousers or skirt have to be purchased from one of the school's suppliers, she says.Both her sons have been through a growth spurt this summer, so she is expecting to spend more than £200 on their branded items alone."I'm just frustrated, for me it's not even about the money," she says."I feel these inconsistencies do not make a difference to education and are really blinkered."But mum-of-five Carol, from Stockport, welcomes the changes at her children's school. She says her son's secondary school only requires a branded blazer, a branded jumper and tie, with everything else available from a range of shops.She tries to get most of her children's uniforms second-hand anyway, but always buys the blazer, which costs around £30, as she likes them to have a new one.She says anything that makes it more affordable for parents is a good thing.But others are not seeing the changes they would like.One father from Oxfordshire, who did not want to be named, says his daughter still has to have seven branded items - three for the uniform, three for PE and a summer polo shirt - as there are no alternatives allowed. "It's ridiculous and unfair. We are paying £200 which we can't afford," he says.Most primary schools already have very few branded items.At Broadhurst Primary, in North Manchester, only the school jumper – and, from 2027, the PE T-shirt – are branded, which the school says brings the total cost of its uniform to £13 per child.Around 23% of secondary schools will have to change their uniform lists for September to comply with the new rules, according to the latest government survey.The education secretary has legal powers to direct schools to comply if they are not sticking to the new rules.One head teachers' union, the Association of School and College Leaders, says the actual difference in cost is likely to be marginal for most families.Its general secretary Pepe Di'Iasio says schools are already trying to balance the cost to parents with maintaining a sense of identity. He says it's also important to keep expensive fashion brands out so no one feels excluded.Some schools have been phasing their changes in over the last few years.King's Oak Academy, in Bristol, has one compulsory item left on its uniform list - a branded PE T-shirt.The school, which goes from reception right through to Year 11, used to have a branded jumper, tie and a shirt, which together cost about £41.Students are now asked to wear a plain polo shirt - which changes colour for the lower, middle and upper school - a sweatshirt or cardigan, and grey skirt or trousers, with all pupils also wearing black trainers. The school says it now costs about £10 to £25, depending on where parents buy the uniform.

schema.headline: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules

title: Mars Bar from the 1990s found during house clearance
description: Honey, they've shrunk our Mars BarsImage source, Victoria GordonImage caption, Now and then... the 1991 Mars Bar alongside one from todayByEleanor Mas
body: Honey, they've shrunk our Mars BarsImage source, Victoria GordonImage caption, Now and then... the 1991 Mars Bar alongside one from todayByEleanor MaslinEast Yorkshire and LincolnshireUpdated 11 minutes agoA 35-year-old Mars Bar has been found during a house clearance – and the discovery has gone viral amid claims it highlights the effect of "shrinkflation".The chocolate bar with a best-before date of 1991 was found during a clear-out of a house in Scunthorpe.Victoria Gordon, who runs the cleaning service, posted a photo on social media of the 62.5g bar alongside one of today's Mars Bars, which is 40g."It was nearly as big as my hand, which was kind of why I noticed it," she said.Image source, Victoria GordonImage caption, Victoria Gordon found the old Mars Bar on 5 AugustSpeaking on BBC Radio Lincolnshire, Gordon said: "We were clearing out a hoarder's house and everything we were rooting through was decades old."This Mars Bar stood out to me because as I picked it up it was nearly the whole length of my hand."I was like, 'Wow, look at the size of that!'"A Mars spokesperson said: "Over the last 35 years, we have made a number of updates to our bar sizes and pack formats to reflect consumer demand, alongside considering wider external factors such as manufacturing costs and the price of cocoa."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, The chocolate was found during a house clearanceGordon, who runs Pocket Rockets, is not sure what she will do with the bar, but she said she might be sitting on a "gold mine"."I do post some hoarding videos but I've never had anything go this viral," she said."It's so fascinating what people find so interesting. I almost put it in the skip [but] I might do a UK tour with it."Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Mars Bar from the 1990s found during house clearance

title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
description: Lucy said she was staying at the hotel in London in October 2025 for "a night away from the fear" following a period of abuse that left her "frightene
body: Lucy said she was staying at the hotel in London in October 2025 for "a night away from the fear" following a period of abuse that left her "frightened and exhausted"."He walked into the hotel and told the receptionist that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. He asked what room I was in and what floor I was staying on," she said.The receptionist handed him a key before directing him upstairs to Lucy's room, she said."I couldn't believe it. The one place I thought he could never get to, he had somehow reached. I felt sick with panic. My safe place disappeared in an instant," she added.She said he physically attacked her and tried to grab her phone.After Lucy convinced her attacker to leave, he returned, "banging, shouting and becoming more aggressive"."I was absolutely terrified. I froze, hoping he would stop. Instead, he kicked the hotel room door off its hinges and forced his way back inside."Travelodge rooms have internal dead-bolt locks on the doors as well as electric key-card operated locks which can be opened from the outside.Lucy said she ran downstairs "shaking, crying and begging for help", adding: "I thought someone would protect me."Instead, Lucy was offered another room in the hotel.Another woman, Jo from Leeds, contacted BBC News following coverage of the Maidenhead attack.In July, she woke in her room to an unknown man standing at the end of her bed, and screamed for help."It was just horrible, it was horrendous. Terrifying. I was shaking so badly," she said.Her friend who was staying in the room heard him say, "I'm sorry, they gave me this key," she said.Jo considered staying elsewhere following the reports of the attack in 2022, but was reassured by Travelodge's chief executive Jo Boydell, who previously said: "The safety and security of customers in our hotels is extremely important and we want everyone to be safe, and feel safe, in our hotels."Jo said: "What happened to us shouldn't have happened. And the assurances [Travelodge] gave are not accurate. The systems are failing."In response, Travelodge said an investigation found "our updated room access security policies, which were in place at the time, were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable."We have retrained the hotel team on our current room security and check-in procedures."Andy Smith, who has travelled the country with his band and stays in dozens of Travelodge hotels a year, said he had been given keys to other people's rooms recently."We went up to the room and there was a guy already asleep in there in a state of undress," he said.It followed another incident about 18 months ago where another man had gained access to his room by telling reception staff he was checking in under a common name such as "Mr Smith", Andy Smith said."I think he just chanced it. Because my name's Smith, I think it's just the pure luck of it. I mean, why wouldn't anyone be asking for ID or anything, like a booking reference or an email address. It beggars belief."Travelodge responded by saying "any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that these incidents should not have happened".A spokesperson for industry group UKHospitality said recent incidents were "extremely serious" and it understood the concerns from guests.It was working with its members to create guidance on customer security which would be published shortly, the spokesperson said."Developed with sector experts, we have continued to engage with ministers on this important work and received positive feedback from government on the work taking place to further bolster guest security," they said.After the Maidenhead sentencing, Travelodge said it had commissioned an independent review led by a barrister "to examine our room access security policies and escalation procedures"."While the independent review is progressing, we have also conducted an internal review and have since made changes to our room access security policy and incident escalation procedures supported by training for all of our customer-facing colleagues."Lucy said the night of her attack had "changed me forever", and she was now unable to stay in hotels because of the fear and anxiety she feels."Hotels need safeguarding procedures... because one mistake can have devastating consequences," she said.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

schema.headline: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room

title: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor cancels live event after plagiarism row
description: The publisher of Arday's memoir Great and Unfortunate Things is going ahead with its release in the US on Tuesday and in the UK on 27 August as planne
body: The publisher of Arday's memoir Great and Unfortunate Things is going ahead with its release in the US on Tuesday and in the UK on 27 August as planned.The book tells the story of his life from being non-verbal until the age of 11 and unable to read or write until 18, then going through a series of "improbable triumphs and heartbreaking setbacks", before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge.However, he has been accused of plagiarism in his PhD thesis, and questions have been raised about the reliability of parts of his life story, including that he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5m for charity.On Wednesday, the University of Cambridge said it had launched an investigation "following new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".Announcing his resignation on the same day, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny had become "too great".He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement."The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

schema.headline: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor cancels live event after plagiarism row
